Hi! I should state the obvious first: I'm just some guy who volunteered to be a mod here, so I will be pretty chill for the most part, and will usually just comment as a regular user. I'll only act like a mod when necessary. I promise to only be drunk with power while offline.

After a brief conversation with my fellow mod, we've decided it's best if the subverse is active from the start in determining the rules of /v/science. And that's what this thread is for. I will make some suggestions for what I imagine the rules might look like, and then we would ask you all to weigh in both on our suggestions and with whatever thoughts you may have of your own.

So. This is the science subverse. A lot of us come from reddit, and /r/science is what I'm basing my thoughts on. Posts that are not at all related to science will of course be removed, as will pseudo-science. Where the line goes between acceptable submissions and overly politicized ones or bad science, however, is a touchy subject for some. We would very much like the community, therefore, to weigh in on just how strict we should be with enforcing high quality submissions. Thus:

Blanket banning of domains: Some domains promote a lot of pseudo-science and bad science, and submissions from them are unlikely to be of high quality. Similar for popular science sites that over-sensationalize everything. Should we enforce blanket bans against such sites? There was some controversy for example regarding an article on infowars.com, which many consider a less than reputable source. We have decided to remove that post. It is the opinion of your almost randomly selected mods that links to infowars should, in fact, not be allowed on /v/science. Many sites are less clear cut, though, and we do not want to be too aggressive with blanket bans, especially not so early in the sub's growth. So my thoughts at the moment are that blanket bans should only be applied in very clear cut cases where most of the community agrees that the sites are bad, and usually only as a response to the same site being submitted several times and being of consistently poor quality. Should we ban a domain or delete a post that many of you think we should not have, we can of course reverse any decision that is too unpopular.

Endorsing other verses on /v/science: We are perfectly fine with new science-related subs advertising their existence on /v/science, especially this early in whoaverse's life. In time we may grow slightly more restrictive, though, in cases where several subs lay claim to the same areas of science, and maybe not all of them look as healthy or high quality as their competitors. Again, should we delete something you feel should not have been deleted, that's a conversation we will have to have together. I will be fairly slow to delete things, though, so this should hopefully not lead to any problems.

General rules: It goes without saying, but we want everyone to be polite in the comment sections. Beyond that, we would like you all to try to keep the titles of your posts from being too sensationalist, and preferably also close to the title of the article you link to. Lastly, on up and down votes: Try to upvote good science even in the comment sections, especially where sources are included. And try to reserve downvotes for bad science, incorrect statements and rudeness. I am sure there will also eventually be a Report button. When it appears, try to reserve it for people who openly insult others, provide extremely bad links (anti-science/pseudo-science/porn/knives cutting into eye balls), and any behaviour that goes against site wide rules.

Tagging: Try to tag posts appropriately with [Biology], [Psychology], etcetera. This will occasionally make it easier for others to find what they are looking for.

There are doubtless questions I did not think to include in the post. Your mods will occasionally make mistakes - be patient with us please. Now it's your turn: What do you want to see or not see included in the rules for this subverse?

(We are now able to delete threads, so that's nice.)

The chief problem with default communities is a very simple one. People are subscribed to a default community without ever indicating an interest in that subject matter. This leads to Christians subscribed to atheist communities, people looking for discussion being bombarded with cat pictures, and a great deal of incompatible mixing of community members. This leads to friction within those communities and makes it more difficult for them to achieve whatever goals they've set for themselves. A subverse's own userbase should not be under a constant stream of attack from disinterested users just joining the site.

It cannot be allowed. There is a far better way, and it's easy.

First, identify a selection of general 'topic areas' that group content together.

For example...

  • television and film
  • music
  • humor
  • politics
  • news
  • science
  • video games
  • sports
  • discussion
  • the whoaverse daily

Next, allow whoaverse communities to indicate which of these groups they think they should be categorized in. Places like music and listentothis go under music. Places like subverseoftheday, newsubverses, ideasforwhoaverse go under the whoaverse daily. News, worldnews go under news. Episodehub, television, gameofthrones, movies all go under film and television. You get the idea.

Subverses must opt-in to this system to be in these categories. They choose their categories during the opt-in process. Site admins can set basic eligibility requirements as necessary.

Now, when a new user creates an account, they are presented with options...

  • help me customize my whoaverse experience
  • not now, remind me later (at next login)
  • I don't want any subscriptions (for bots or users who want to roll their own)

For those who choose to customize, show them the broad list of categories, and allow them to check a box next to those categories. They are subscribed to the subverses that are part of any category they select, up to the maximum subscription limit (and there shouldn't be one of those, ideally - or it should be high, not a pathetic 100 like reddit's maximum).

This does require work from the site administrators from time to time maintaining the categories themselves. A subverse can be set up to allow the community to decide the categories and discuss what should and shouldn't be in each one, they can simply make suggestions to the admins from time to time when a beneficial change is identified.

This provides a completely organic system that can evolve over time, is sculpted by user feedback yet curated by administrators, and will prevent anyone from ever being subscribed to a verse on a topic that they haven't selected themselves. I think this is an ideal solution that will sort new users into places they will be happy with extreme efficiency.
On the nature of default communities, and a better way to manage them!
